items.title: Supreme Court says no punitive action against law student accused of instigating fellow students to join CJP dharna
items.summary: The Supreme Court on Monday ordered that no punitive action be taken against law student Akshat Tripathi based on a ₹5 lakh bond notice issued to him by Uttar Pradesh (UP) authorities over the Cockroach Janta Party protests. A bench of Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana passed the direction after the UP government told the Court today that the notice has been withdrawn. "That being so, it is directed that action, if any, taken in the past pursuant to the notice dated September 4 stands annulled. Consequently, no punitive action of any nature shall be taken against the petitioner," the Court said. By way of background, the notice dated September 4 was issued under Section 130 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) by the Executive Magistrate-Third, Greater Noida. It called upon Tripathi to show cause why he should not be bound under with a personal bond of ₹5 lakh and two sureties of like amount, for allegedly instigating fellow students to join a proposed CJP dharna. The notice came three days after the Supreme Court's September 1 order quashing cases against students who took part in the CJP-led protests against exam paper leaks.

The Court also issued notice to co-accused Vinod Tomar who has also been acquitted in the case. The wrestlers approached the sessions court against the magistrate court's order of August 3 acquitting Singh and Tomar. According to their appeal, the trial court order is based on "surmises and conjectures" and its reasoning is based on "archaic and stereotypical assumptions" about the “expected” behaviour of victims of sexual assault and harassment. As per the plea, the trial court fixated on small, unimportant slips and used them to reject the case against Singh in its entirety, instead of looking at the whole picture backed up by witness corroboration. The Bench observed that animals experience pain, stress and fear like humans, while noting that the existing legal framework continues to treat animals largely as objects or property. It also expressed concern over the penalties prescribed under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960, observing that fines for certain acts of cruelty can be as low as ₹10 to ₹50. items.title: Government can invoke compulsory licensing under Patents Act to make breast cancer drugs affordable: Kerala High Court
items.summary: The Kerala High Court on Monday suggested that the Central government could invoke its powers under Section 100 of the Patents Act, 1970 (Act), to improve access to heavily priced patented breast cancer medicines [ In Re Exorbitant Pricing of Life Saving Patented Medicines ] Justice Harisankar V Menon , however, left the final decision on this matter to the Central government, terming it a policy decision. "It is for the Central Government to consider whether Section 100 of the (Patents) Act requires to be invoked since ultimately the same is a policy decision, " the Court said. Section 100 allows the central government to authorise the use of patented invention for government purposes, even without the patent holder's consent. The Court observed that Section 100 could be invoked by the government to increase access to expensive medicines for needy patients, on a non-commercial basis.
